name: Cinematic
basis: film grading conventions: teal-orange split tone, bloom, widescreen bars (how)
note: Anamorphic streak and grain are device and film garnish; the look is digital grading.

lumenary.blurb: A frame from a feature film: shadows pulled toward teal and skin toward orange, a soft bloom, blue streaks drawn sideways from the brightest lights, grain and black bars.

facts.bestOn: People, and scenes with lights in the frame

why: A film frame is recognised by a few habits. Skin is warm and everything else leans cool, because orange and teal sit opposite each other and make a face stand out. Bright lights bloom, and through an anamorphic lens they throw a blue streak across the frame. There is grain. And the picture is wider than a television, which the black bars announce.
how: Set the saturation, then tint the shadows one way and the highlights another.
Add contrast with an S-shaped curve.
Blur the bright parts and blend them back as a warm bloom.
Smear only the brightest lights sideways and add them in blue.
Darken the corners and add grain, strongest in the mid tones.
Add black bars, and a subtitle if you write one.
history: CinemaScope arrived in 1953 with The Robe, squeezing a wide picture onto ordinary film with an anamorphic lens, and the streaked highlights of such lenses became part of the look. Colour was once set in the laboratory. In 2000 O Brother, Where Art Thou? became the first feature graded entirely on a computer, and the control that gave led, within a decade, to the teal and orange palette of blockbuster cinema.
terms: Adjusting the colour and contrast of a film after it is shot.
A lens that squeezes a wide view sideways onto the film, to be stretched again on projection.
Tinting shadows and highlights with different colours.
paragraphs: A film grade moves colour by tone. Saturation is set first, by scaling each channel’s distance from the pixel’s brightness. Then comes split toning: one tint is added to the shadows and another to the highlights, with weights that are the squares of darkness and of brightness, so mid tones are barely touched. In the default grade the shadows gain blue and green and the highlights gain red, which sets skin, which is orange, against everything else. An S-shaped curve about mid grey adds contrast.

Lenses and film add the rest. Bloom isolates the bright parts, blurs them widely and blends them back in a warm tone. Streaks use a stricter mask of only the brightest lights and blur it along the rows alone, three times, which approximates a wide Gaussian in one direction; the result is added in blue, as a cylindrical anamorphic lens smears a point of light into a horizontal line. Corners are darkened, and grain is made strongest in the mid tones. The bars bring the frame toward the chosen shape, but each stops at one eighth of the height so an upright picture is not reduced to a strip.

equations.note: Split toning: s and h are the shadow and highlight tints, l the brightness, k the grade strength.
Contrast: a blend toward the smoothstep curve; c is the grade’s contrast times k.
Height of each black bar for a frame of ratio ρ, when the picture is taller than that ratio.

presets.text: Bleach bypass with heavy grain is a war film.
Golden hour with strong bloom and no bars flatters a portrait.
Add a line of dialogue to finish the frame.
